title: Calgary mother suing for son's 'negligent' death in Saskatchewan prison
article: The mother of a Calgary man killed in a Saskatchewan prison is hoping to spark change in the correctional system with a new lawsuit claiming her son should have been allowed to enter drug treatment instead of being carted back to jail for a drug overdose.

Lauren Laithwaite is seeking damages from the city, police, the attorney general of Canada, Correctional Services Canada and Alberta Health Services for "negligence" and "false imprisonment" she says led to the 2017 in-custody death of her son, Christopher Van Camp.

But the action is more than just an $11-million lawsuit for the grieving mother, who says there's only one thing she wants from the civil suit: "Change" in a correctional system that Laithwaite said denied her son addiction treatment and put him in a cell with a violent offender now accused of Van Camp's murder.

"They put my son in there. My son was killed after four hours (of being put back in prison) ... we're going almost two years and I don't even have a plea yet," Lathwaite said of Correctional Services Canada and Tyler Vandewater, the cellmate charged with the second-degree murder of Van Camp.

Christopher Andrew Van Camp, 37, died June 7, 2017 while in custody at the Saskatchewan Penitentiary in Prince Albert, Sask. His mother Lauren Laithwaite is suing the City of Calgary, the Calgary Police Service, Alberta Health Services and the Attorney General through Correctional Services Canada for negligence and false imprisonment she says lead to her son's murder.
Laithwaite said her son had a history of drug abuse but was determined to get clean when he was granted parole on April 24, 2017.
She said before his release, Van Camp was "caught with drugs in prison" and told his parole officer he regularly had access to drugs while incarcerated.
Laithwaite said she's met "a number of parents" whose children overdosed while in custody, saying there is a "fundamental problem" with "a prison system that can't keep drugs out."
But an overdose on cocaine laced with fentanyl exactly one month after his parole landed Van Camp in hospital, where he spent five days in a coma before he awoke with severe health complications.
"He had lost muscle mass and was limited in his physical strength and dexterity," reads a statement of claim filed last week. "He also had breathing issues, which often resulted in coughing fits."
While still in hospital, Laithwaite said her son's parole officer had arranged for Van Camp to go into treatment for his addiction once he recovered.

But members of the Calgary Police Service arrested her son for breaching his parole conditions for using drugs, sending him back to prison while Van Camp was still in a weakened state, Laithwaite said.

And in her statement of claim, Laithwaite contends her son should never have been returned to custody at the Saskatchewan Penitentiary and said there was a "failing to transport Chris in a properly sanctioned and equipped medical vehicle" by CSC.

Christopher Andrew Van Camp, 37, while in a coma after an overdose in 2017. Van Camp's mother, Lauren Laithwaite, said her son should not have been sent back to jail after his overdose under the Good Samaritan Drug Overdose act.

Under the Good Samaritan Drug Overdose Act, no one who calls 911 because they or someone else is overdosing will be charged with violating release conditions if the evidence was found as a result of seeking medical assistance.

The Good Samaritan act only came into place less than three weeks before Van Camp's arrest in hospital. Laithwaite alleges a parole manager "overruled" the act and an earlier decision to admit Van Camp to drug treatment.

"Nobody did their job," she said of three CPS officers who arrested her son and cuffed "him to his bed," the parole manager who denied his drug treatment and AHS employees who failed "to protect their patient ... from false arrest."
Van Camp was found unresponsive in his cell the morning on June 7, 2017, just hours after he was transferred to the maximum security unit at the Prince Albert, Sask. facility.
Laithwaite claims mandatory hourly prisoner checks failed to discover Van Camp was dead for at least six hours.

Van Camp had been serving a sentence at the Saskatchewan Penitentiary in Prince Albert since 2012. Calgary police had previously issued 18 warrants for his arrest related to domestic violence offences.
After firing three lawyers since 2017, Laithwaite said Vandewater will be back in court to face the second-degree murder charge in March.
